chunks: My scholars narrated to me from Muḥammad ibn Yaḥyā al-‘Aṭṭār, from al-Ḥusayn ibn ‘Abdillāh, from al-Ḥasan ibn ‘Alī ibn Abī ‘Uthmān, from al-Ḥasan ibn ‘Alī ibn ‘Abdillāh ibn al-Mughīrah, from Abī ‘Umārah al-Munshid, who said:

Whenever al-Ḥusayn (peace be upon him) was mentioned in front of Abī ‘Abdillāh (peace be upon him) during the day, Abī ‘Abdillāh (peace be upon him) would be seen smiling until nightfall. And he (peace be upon him) used to say: 'Al-Ḥusayn (peace be upon him) is the tear of every believer.'

key_terms.أَبُو عَبْدِ اللَّهِ: Abu Abdillah; a title for Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq (peace be upon him)
key_terms.الْحُسَيْنُ: Al-Husayn; referring to Imam al-Husayn ibn Ali (peace be upon him)
key_terms.عَبْرَة: Tear; metaphorically referring to the emotional response or weeping associated with remembrance
key_terms.مُتَبَسِّماً: Smiling; showing a gentle, joyful expression

ai.seo_question: What is the significance of Imam al-Husayn being called the 'tear of every believer'?
ai.summary: In Kamil al-Ziyarat, Ibn Qulawayh records Imam al-Ṣādiq’s (a.s.) consistent smile upon hearing al-Ḥusayn’s name, illustrating that the memory of the Martyr brings spiritual joy (faraj) rather than solely sorrow. The phrase 'al-Ḥusayn 'abratu kulli mu'min' (al-Ḥusayn is the tear of every believer) establishes a theological link between the Imam’s martyrdom and the believer’s inner state of humility and love, a concept central to Shia devotional practice. This narration underscores that remembrance (dhikr) of al-Ḥusayn serves as a means of connecting with the divine through the affective experience of the Ahl al-Bayt.
